new_statements.quote: Les langues sous étude ont deux tons simples et deux tons complexes. Nous choisissons de ne pas noter les tons bas, mais seulement les tons haut ´, montants ˇ ou descendants ˆ.
new_statements.translation: The languages under study have two simple tones and two complex tones. We choose not to mark low tones, but only high ´, rising ˇ or falling ˆ tones.

Les langues sous étude ont deux tons simples et deux tons complexes. Nous choisissons de ne pas noter les tons bas, mais seulement les tons haut ´, montants ˇ ou descendants ˆ." It hangs on the first Mokpá example in (3a) 'kokpéka'. A a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for accent/stress/tonal/ton(s)/prosod/pénult finds no other prosodic statement (the only other hits are 'structure syllabique' in a table heading, 'accentués' in the ordinary sense in fn. 11, and Spa 1973 'Traits et tons en enya' in the references), so the reading tone language, no stress stat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mokpa is a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (rising, falling); the source makes no statement about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress discussion at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Footnote covering all three languages jointly (ɛnyá, mokpá, metóko) in a comparative article on labial-velars; it explains the tone-marking convention for the cited lexical items (citation forms in a comparative wordlist). Word stress is never mentioned anywhere in the article.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog mokp1238 'Mokpa' has no ISO code. Kopa wa Kopa & Ricquier 2023 call the language mokpá 'aussi dénommé kileka', give it Guthrie code D142 and place it with ɛnyá (D14, gey) and metóko/Mituku (D13, zmq) in a branch of the Lega subgroup; speakers live on the right bank of the Lualaba hemmed in by Kómo forest, with a group on Bamanga island near Ubundu. Glottolog's own bib note on Motingea 1990 says Mokpa 'aka Waleka.. closest to Mituku and possibly identical to it', but the 2023 authors, using the first author's field data, treat Mokpa and Metóko as separate languages. The quoted tone statement covers ɛnyá, mokpá and metóko jointly.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement (Kopa wa Kopa & Ricquier 2023, fn. 7: two simple + two complex tones, no stress statement) that Mokpa is a tone language with no statement on stress. Adds nothing on stress. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; this work does not supply one. The blogpost is by the same field team, describes the language as a whole ('Mokpa does not show significant dialectal variation'), and its literature overview confirms the only other published source is Motingea Mangulu 1990 (print-only) plus two unpublished ISP mémoires the authors themselves could not consult.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work says only that Mokpa has a two-way tone contrast; it says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The blogpost describes Mokpa as spoken in 15 villages on the right bank of the Lualaba from Batikalela to Tubundubundu (Ubundu Territory), autonym Mokpa/Cenamokpa, exonym (Ba)leka/Kileka; it states explicitly that the language shows no significant dialectal variation and proposes the Bantu code D15 (replacing D142 used in the 2023 article). The 'two-tone distinction' sentence refers to the language as a whole, not to a particular dialect.

sources.quote: Les langues sous étude ont deux tons simples et deux tons complexes. Nous choisissons de ne pas noter les tons bas, mais seulement les tons haut ´, montants ˇ ou descendants ˆ.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Only prosodic statement is fn. 7 (p. 8): the three languages (ɛnyá, mokpá, metóko) have two simple tones and two complex tones; low tone left unmarked, high, rising and falling marked. Comparative article on labial-velar consonants; §2 gives Mokpa's location, classification (D142, Lega subgroup, 'aussi dénommé kileka') and notes that the three languages are poorly documented (at most five grammatical/lexical titles each, only sketches and limited lexicons). Cites Motingea 1990 and Abuka 2021 as the prior descriptions.
